title: Census Geography Finder: Tract, County, State
description: Find the census geography containing a point with the Census Geography Finder — state, county, tract and block group FIPS codes. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a point in downtown Chicago resolves to Illinois (FIPS 17), Cook County (17031), and then one specific tract and block group inside it — the full nesting doll of US census geography.
quick_answer: The Census Geography Finder reports the census geography that contains a coordinate point — state, county, census tract, block group and block, with their FIPS codes. Paste the point and read the hierarchy: the identifiers that unlock every dataset the Census Bureau and the ACS publish.

and tract-level tables can join on them.
Funders ask for tract identifiers because tracts are the unit of need measurement (CRA, CDFI and health research all speak tract). This finder is step one of a thousand applications.
A claimed tract for an address can be checked from its coordinates in one lookup — mismatches usually mean a geocode landed across the street, in the next tract.
Nation, state, county, tract, block group, block — the nesting is the Bureau's master design, and seeing your own home's full stack teaches it permanently.

A block-group GEO ID like 170310101001 reads as: 17 (Illinois) + 031 (Cook County) + 010100 (tract) + 1 (block group). The finder returns the stack labelled, so the code stops being a phone number and becomes an address in geography-space.

Tracts are drawn for roughly 4,000 residents (the Census Bureau's design target is an average near 4,000, within a 1,200–8,000 range); block groups hold 600–3,000. The finder shows you units that were designed to be statistically comparable — that is their whole purpose.

rows: A city block or rural equivalent
popular_table.note: Boundaries and codes are the Census Bureau's TIGER/Line geography for the stated vintage; tracts are redrawn each decennial census, so a 2010 tract ID and a 2020 tract ID are different objects with similar names.

faq: Which census vintage does it use?

The finder reports the current TIGER/Line geography it is built on and names the vintage with the result — because tract IDs silently change meaning between censuses, the vintage is part of the answer.
Does it cover Puerto Rico and the territories?
Census geography covers Puerto Rico's municipios in the same hierarchy; the island areas use their own census programmes and vintages, stated with any result.
Louisiana parishes, Alaska boroughs, independent cities and DC function as counties in census geography — the finder uses the Bureau's list, names included.
Can I get the tract for an address, not coordinates?
Geocode the address first (the Batch Geocoder), then find its geography. The two-step route keeps each tool's honesty about its own step.
Why did my tract change between 2010 and 2020?
Tracts split when population grows past the design range and merge when it falls — your neighbourhood did not move; the statistical net was re-knotted.
The Bureau maintains American Indian area geographies alongside the standard stack; where a point falls in one, the fuller record matters for the programmes that fund by it.
Is the block my exact address's unit?
Blocks are the smallest geography and hold no published demographics (privacy). Your block ID identifies geography, never your household's data — by the Bureau's design.
